name: Carlos Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Fenwick Estate, nine hundred hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape, plus a small flock of sheep that graze the cover crops in winter. The land's owned by an investment company in the city, and I answer to a man called Gerald who visits twice a year in very clean boots. This time of year I'm planning next season's rotation, which crop goes in which field, and selling grain from the store. There's me, two full-time operators, and a contractor at harvest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's a typical day right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Seven o'clock I check the grain prices on my phone, then I walk the stores to check the moisture probes. Then it's the office for an hour, the spray plans, the sales. Afternoons I'm usually out in the fields looking at the crops or with Viktor on the drill. I like it best when the numbers and the field agree with each other, which is rarer than you'd think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Quite a lot, by farm standards. The tractors steer themselves by GPS to within two centimetres, and we have yield maps, which show which parts of a field grew well. I use an AI chat tool sometimes, mostly to summarise the long market reports. I didn't touch it until the merchant's rep showed me how he used it. I'm not first, but I'm not last.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Lower than it should be for the size of the job. The company says the margins are thin, which is true. We've got the mortgage, Ines's wage from the bank, and about three weeks of savings. That's enough until it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool if you use it with your eyes open. At the discussion group I'd say I use it for market reports and it saves me an hour a week. Nobody would argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's about neutral for me. My returns depend on the grain price, the weather and the cost of fertiliser. A better search engine helps at the edges, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it more for the planning, maybe get it to compare spray costs from the three suppliers. Maybe save a few hundred a year. And I'd keep doing what I'm doing, which is getting more out of every hectare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly pleased, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said three weeks of savings is enough until it isn't. When was the last time it wasn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago, Ines was off sick for two months, and the bank paid her less while she was off. We went into the overdraft by about two thousand. It took us a year to climb back out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Gerald think of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He thinks I'm reliable, which is what he wants. He doesn't really know what I do. He knows the profit per hectare and the number at the bottom, and as long as that's above the neighbours, he leaves me alone.

S0.say: I'd say it's a decent tool if you use it with your eyes open. At the discussion group I'd mention it saves me an hour a week on market reports, and nobody would argue.
S0.think: I think it's about neutral for me, since my returns depend on grain prices, weather and fertiliser costs. A better search engine only helps at the edges.
S0.do: Uses AI more for planning, such as comparing spray costs from three suppliers to save a few hundred a year. Keeps working to get more out of every hectare.
S0.quote: He knows the profit per hectare and the number at the bottom, and as long as that's above the neighbours, he leaves me alone.
S0.fieldNote: He thinks in margins and per-hectare returns, and he's comfortable with tools once someone has shown him the way. The overdraft story from his wife's illness shows how close the edge is. His relationship with the absent owner is distant but steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the second. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible, change at a pace people can keep up with. But I'd also say if firms stop hiring beginners, we'll pay for it in twenty years when nobody knows how to do anything. That's not left or right, that's just maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the company would use it to watch me more closely. Every field, every decision, compared with a model in an office. They'd start asking why I sprayed on Tuesday and not Wednesday. That's the kind of slow pressure that grinds you down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever system the company brings in, once Viktor or the neighbours had tried it. I'd keep my own records, field by field, so I can show my reasons. And I'd ask Gerald for a pay review, pointing out that I'm now doing the job of a manager and a data person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Not about the work, about being watched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask for a pay review. Have you done that before, and how did it go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years ago. I got two percent and a bottle of whisky at Christmas. This time I'd have numbers, I'd show the yield against the regional average. I'm in the top fifth, which is the kind of thing an investment company understands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, if fewer beginners got hired?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Viktor's son, Andrei. He's nineteen and he wants to be an agronomist, the person who advises on crops. That's exactly the kind of job a computer will do first. I've told him to get his hands dirty as well, so he's got both.

S1.say: I'd say slow change at a pace people can follow is sensible. But if firms stop hiring beginners we'll pay in twenty years, and that's not left or right, it's just maths.
S1.think: I think the company would use it to watch me more closely, comparing every field decision with a model in an office. That slow pressure would grind me down.
S1.do: Learns the company's new system once colleagues or neighbours have tried it, keeps his own field-by-field records to justify decisions, and asks for a pay review backed by top-fifth yield figures.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, about being watched rather than about the work.
S1.quote: They'd start asking why I sprayed on Tuesday and not Wednesday.
S1.fieldNote: His centre politics show in how he frames things: not left or right, just maths. His fear isn't losing the job but being second-guessed by a model. He would meet the company on its own terms, with numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan, not shouting. Retraining, some support for people who lose jobs, and the firms making the money chipping in, but without making the country a place nobody wants to invest in. Both sides have a point and neither will admit it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one's about Ines. She's at the bank, in the branch, doing mortgages and accounts. That's exactly the routine office work on the card. If she goes, we lose half our income and the mortgage is in trouble within three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Ines and go through every bill. We'd cut the second car, the streaming, Lucas's guitar lessons if we had to. She'd start looking at other work straight away, maybe at the agricultural merchant, which still needs people who know money. I'd ask Gerald if there was any extra work on the estate, the holiday cottages maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm a numbers person and I can see the numbers don't work without her wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd cut Lucas's guitar lessons. How would you tell him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight. He's fifteen, he'd understand. He'd sulk for a week and then teach himself off videos, probably better than the lessons. Marta would be harder, she's eleven, she'd think it's her fault somehow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ines working at the merchant. Has she ever talked about leaving the bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never. She likes it, the regulars, the old ladies who bring her cake. That's what I'd feel worst about. It's not just the money, it's that she'd lose her place in town.

S2.say: I'd say we need a plan, not shouting: retraining, support and contributions from the firms profiting, without scaring off investment. Both sides have a point and neither will admit it.
S2.think: I think this is about my partner, who does routine work at a bank branch. If she loses her job we lose half our income, and the mortgage is in trouble within three months.
S2.do: Goes through every bill with his partner in the first month, cutting the second car, streaming and possibly his son's guitar lessons. Helps her look for work at the agricultural merchant and asks about extra estate work.
S2.feel: Anxious, because the numbers don't work without his partner's wage.
S2.quote: It's not just the money, it's that she'd lose her place in town.
S2.fieldNote: For him this scenario is about his partner, and his numbers-first approach meets something money can't measure: her place in the community. He plans calmly but clearly sees the cliff edge. His parenting answers were warm and specific.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains have to be shared, but carefully. Some tax on the people who've done well out of shares and houses, yes, but don't wreck the economy over it. I'd probably say less than I think, because the estate is owned by exactly the kind of people who are winning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Ines is gone, and so is half our town's office work. Physical jobs are fine, the card says, so I'm the one keeping the family going on a lower wage. And the company that owns the estate gets richer with every jump in land prices, and that money never reaches me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move Ines onto the farm side, the estate's holiday cottages or the farm accounts if Gerald would pay her. I'd look for a second income, maybe drilling and spraying for neighbours on the weekends, which could bring in five hundred a month. I'd talk to the bank about stretching the mortgage before we missed a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, heavier than before. Like walking a crop after a hailstorm, counting the damage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd say less than you think. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Gerald's company owns the roof over my job. If I go on about taxing investors, I'm talking about my boss. I'm not proud of that, but I've got a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Weekend contracting on top of a full job. When would you sleep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sleep in winter. That's farming. My dad did two jobs for ten years when I was small, and I don't remember him much from those years, which I think about.

S3.say: I'd say gains must be shared carefully, with some tax on those who've won from shares and houses but without wrecking the economy. I'd say less than I think, since the estate's owners are among the winners.
S3.think: I think my partner's job and half the town's office work would go, leaving me supporting the family on a low wage. The estate's owners grow richer as land prices jump, and none of that reaches me.
S3.do: Tries to move his partner into estate work such as holiday cottages or farm accounts, adds weekend drilling and spraying for neighbours for about five hundred a month, and asks the bank to stretch the mortgage early.
S3.feel: Anxious and heavier, like counting damage after a hailstorm.
S3.quote: Because Gerald's company owns the roof over my job. If I go on about taxing investors, I'm talking about my boss.
S3.fieldNote: The gap between say and think is widest here, and he named it himself: he softens his public view because his employer is one of the winners. His memory of his father working two jobs gives his weekend plan a sad edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules on how fast this happens and who pays for the people left behind. I'd say it at the farmers' union meeting and in a letter to the paper, and I'd try to sound reasonable, because shouting gets you nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think arable is next in line. The tractors already steer themselves. A robot sprayer and a self-driving combine, and the company needs one person with a laptop for nine hundred hectares. Maybe that's me, maybe it's a younger man for less, or maybe it's someone in the city watching ten estates at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make sure I'm the one who knows the robots best on the estate, once the first neighbours had them working. I'd ask Gerald for a written plan and a contract with notice. And I'd start looking at jobs fixing the machines, with the dealer, because someone has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the first year of a drought, when you can see where it's going and can't stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe it's someone in the city watching ten estates. How real does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very real. The company already gets the yield maps sent to the city each week. I've seen a pilot in another country where one agronomist watched forty farms from a screen. The farm managers there are now called site supervisors and earn less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With Ines already out of work in this picture, what would you tell the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd be all right, which I wouldn't know. Lucas would see through it. I'd probably tell him the truth later, on the tractor, where it's easier to talk without looking at each other.

S4.say: I'd say we need rules on how fast this happens and who pays for those left behind. I'd say it at the farmers' union and in a letter to the paper, keeping it reasonable.
S4.think: I think arable farming is next, since tractors already steer themselves. With robot sprayers and self-driving combines, nine hundred hectares need one person with a laptop, and it might be someone in the city watching ten estates.
S4.do: Aims to be the estate's best robot operator once neighbours have them running, asks Gerald for a written plan and a notice contract, and looks into machine repair work with the dealer.
S4.feel: Alarmed, like the first year of a drought you can see coming and can't stop.
S4.quote: I'd probably tell him the truth later, on the tractor, where it's easier to talk without looking at each other.
S4.fieldNote: He would still adapt, but the threat of remote management from the city genuinely frightens him. He had a real example in mind, which made it concrete. The line about talking to his son on the tractor was quietly moving.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one with robots, because it takes both of us, Ines and me, within a few years. With no savings and a mortgage, we'd be choosing between bad options. What would help is a proper transition, notice, retraining paid for while you still have a wage, and something to stop the bank taking the house while you're in between.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the land. Everyone talks about who owns the robots, but on an estate like mine, it's the owners of the land who'll decide. Nobody asks them in surveys like this.

headlineQuote: Because Gerald's company owns the roof over my job. If I go on about taxing investors, I'm talking about my boss.
portrait: Carlos Weber, 43, manages a nine-hundred-hectare grain and oilseed estate for a city investment company, on modest pay and with about three weeks of savings. He thinks in numbers and per-hectare returns, uses GPS steering and the odd AI tool, and adopts new things once others have shown they work. His centre politics make him reach for reasonable plans, but he admits he says less than he thinks because his employer is among the winners. His worry moves from being watched by models, to his partner's bank job, to remote robot farming that could leave both of them out of work.
biggestWorry: The fast AI and robots scenario, because it could take both his partner's job and his own within a few years while they have no savings and a mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A proper transition with notice and retraining paid while still earning, and protection from losing the house while between jobs.
